hints: Recall what each level of protein structure describes - primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary. Which level is only found in some proteins and not others?
walkthrough:
What quaternary really means**
Think of a protein chain as one long string of amino acids. Primary, secondary and tertiary structure all describe folding within a single string. Quaternary is different - it only exists when two or more separate strings join together to make one functional molecule.

Apply to the antibody in Fig. 3.1**
Look at the Y-shape. It is not one chain. It is built from four separate polypeptides - two longer heavy chains in the middle and two shorter light chains on the outside, held together by disulfide bonds. Because there is more than one polypeptide in the finished molecule, it has quaternary structure.
Final answer: It is made up of more than one polypeptide chain.

hints: Look at the top of the Y in Fig. 3.1 where the variable regions are labelled. How many separate tips are there for binding, and what is their job?
Think about why one antibody binds only one type of antigen. What idea about shape links a binding site to its antigen, like an enzyme to its substrate?
Now link that shape back to protein structure. What level of structure varies between antibodies to create a different shape each time?
walkthrough:
Two binding sites at the tips**
The variable regions at the two arms of the Y form two antigen-binding sites. Their function is to bind antigen during the immune response.

Complementary shape gives specificity**
The 3D shape of each binding site is complementary to the shape of one specific antigen / epitope. That is why each antibody is specific and will only bind that one antigen shape.

Why the shape is variable**
That different shape comes from a different primary structure - a different sequence of amino acids and so different R-groups / side chains - in the variable region of each different antibody. Different R-groups interact differently to fold into a different binding-site shape.

Final answer: Variable regions form two antigen-binding sites; shape is complementary to the specific antigen / epitope, giving specificity; determined by sequence of amino acids / R-groups in the variable region.

hints: The variable end binds antigen, so think about the other end. Once the antibody is stuck to a pathogen, what immune cell needs to find and grip it?
walkthrough:
The handle end of the antibody**
Think of the antibody as having two jobs. The variable tips grab the pathogen. The constant stem at the bottom acts as a handle for the rest of the immune system.

Link to phagocytosis**
That constant region binds to receptors on phagocytes such as macrophages and neutrophils. This helps the phagocyte recognise and engulf the antibody-antigen complex.
Final answer: Binds to receptors on phagocytes, e.g. macrophages / neutrophils.

hints: To get antibody-producing cells, you must first make an animal produce them. What would you inject into a small mammal like a mouse to start the immune response?
Antibody-producing B-lymphocytes die quickly in culture, while cancerous myeloma cells divide forever but make no useful antibody. How could combining them solve both problems?
After fusion you have many mixed cells. What must you do to pick out the one cell making exactly the antibody you want and make many identical copies of it?
For full marks you need a logical sequence from start to large-scale production. What final step lets you make enough antibody for medical use?
walkthrough:
Immunise the mouse**
The target antigen is injected into a small mammal, usually a mouse. This triggers an immune response so its B-lymphocytes make the desired antibody.

Collect the B-cells**
B-lymphocytes / plasma cells / splenocytes are removed, usually from the spleen or lymph nodes. These cells make the right antibody but cannot survive long or divide continuously in culture.

Fuse to make a hybridoma**
These B-cells are fused, using PEG or electrofusion, with myeloma / cancer cells that divide indefinitely. The fused hybridoma cell now has both properties: it makes the specific antibody and divides continuously.

Screen, clone and scale up**
Hybridomas are screened / tested to find the one producing the desired antibody. That cell is cloned to give a population of identical cells, then grown in large scale / fermenter to produce large quantities of identical monoclonal antibodies.

Final answer: Antigen injected into small mammal; antibody-producing B-lymphocytes / plasma cells isolated from spleen; fused with myeloma cells to form hybridoma cells; desired hybridoma screened / cloned and grown in large scale / fermenter to produce monoclonal antibodies.

hints: The word monoclonal means from one clone. What does that tell you about the specificity of every antibody in the sample compared with normal serum?
If every antibody binds only one epitope and can carry a visible tag, how could that help you find tiny amounts of a pathogen or tell two similar strains apart?
walkthrough:
One specificity only**
Because they come from one clone, all monoclonal antibodies have the same specificity and detect only one antigen / epitope. Normal antibodies are a mixture, so they are less precise.

Why that helps diagnosis**
This allows them to distinguish between different pathogens or strains of a pathogen, even when they are very similar. They can be labelled / tagged, e.g. with a fluorescent label, so the location of cancer cells, blood clots or infection can be detected quickly and in very small amounts.
Final answer: All have same specificity / bind only one antigen / epitope; can distinguish between pathogens / strains; can be labelled to locate antigen / give fast diagnosis.
